name: CENTURY ALUMINUM

priced.reason: not a repriceable fcff name or no growth supplied

devils_advocate.strongest_counter: That I am refusing the cheapest name I have seen on this screen. The engine says -90.8% and the 23rd percentile of Materials, i.e. expensive; that is demonstrably an artifact, and once corrected the name trades at 2.4x annualised adjusted EBITDA and about 4.2x annualised free cash flow with $713M of cash and $1.16bn of liquidity. Correcting a false sell into a buy is exactly what this engine exists to do, and the HNI precedent of 2026-10-09 is a direct template: a defect running toward a false sell, corrected from the company's own filed numbers, recorded cheap.
devils_advocate.what_would_prove_it: Whether the 2026 earnings level is a plateau or a spike. The observable is the realised price path and the Q4/Q1 prints against the $275-300M guide, plus any decision on the Oklahoma smelter and its capital call.
devils_advocate.already_visible: Yes, and the counter loses on it, which is why this is no_edge and not cheap. Three pieces of evidence are already on the page. First, the same company produced $82.3M of nine-month operating cash flow in 2025 and $630.9M in 2026 — a 7.7x swing with no change in the asset base beyond restarts, which is the definition of a price-driven peak rather than an earnings base. Second, management has already guided the next quarter DOWN 10-17%, and a company guiding down off a record quarter is telling you the quarter was not repeatable (the DORM test). Third, and the piece the HNI template lacks: the profit is policy. The release names Section 232, the 45X credits inside operating cash flow, and the administration's proposed tariff REDUCTION in the same document. HNI's correction rested on an ASC 805 pro forma — a filed, audited fact about a combined business. Here the correction rests on extrapolating a tariff regime. Those are not the same quality of evidence.
devils_advocate.unresolved: The capital intensity of the growth, which is the whole bear case and is undisclosed: management has not sized Century's own share of the new smelter, and the Motley Fool coverage of the call frames it the same way — 'a pending Oklahoma smelter decision leaves Century's cash-rich balance sheet facing a key question: how much capital will growth actually require?' I also cannot size the Hurricane Melissa impact on Jamalco, and I am relying on financial statements carrying an UNREMEDIATED material weakness with an adverse auditor opinion on internal control.

what_changed: The engine's inputs are a year out of date and the current year is a different business. The 2026-11-05 Q3 10-Q reports nine-month operating cash flow of $630.9M against capex of $172.2M — free cash flow of $458.7M, against an FCFF base of $18.1M. Nine-month net income attributable to Century is $889.4M against $40.0M. Q3 alone: net sales $961.2M, net income $302.6M, adjusted EBITDA $331.6M, driven by the restart of Line 2 at Grundartangi returning to near full production and favourable realised metal prices, with Mt. Holly restarted too. Cash went from $134.2M at 2025-12-31 to $713.0M, and liquidity is $1,161.5M. Three qualifiers arrived with it: Q4 adjusted EBITDA is guided to $275-300M, i.e. DOWN 10-17% sequentially; Hurricane Melissa struck Jamalco in late October and the restart is still in progress; and 45X advanced-manufacturing tax-credit receipts are explicitly named as a contributor to operating cash flow, so part of the cash is a legislated policy transfer rather than operating margin. Separately, capex has already more than doubled to $172.2M for nine months from $65.1M on the Mt. Holly restart.
consensus_case: The market is paying $2.98bn for a primary aluminium smelter that earned $889.4M attributable to shareholders in nine months — about 2.5x annualised earnings and roughly 2.4x annualised adjusted EBITDA of $1.25bn. That is not an oversight; it is what the market always pays at a commodity peak, and the peak here is extreme and policy-dependent. The same company generated $40.0M of nine-month net income and $82.3M of nine-month operating cash flow ONE YEAR EARLIER. Management has already guided Q4 adjusted EBITDA down to $275-300M from $331.6M. The margin rests on Section 232 tariffs supporting the US Midwest premium, and the company's own release flags that the administration is proposing to REDUCE aluminium tariffs for parties committing to new US capacity. On top of that sits a greenfield smelter — the first in the US in over 45 years — with $500M of DOE funding and a possible Emirates Global Aluminium joint venture, which is where the cash is going. The market is refusing to capitalise a tariff-supported peak into perpetuity, and that refusal is defensible.
base_case_rationale: No number is recordable, because the base spans a factor of six and the sign of the answer sits inside it. The engine's $18.1M is not a cash-flow estimate at all: mean(cfo-less-capex) over the window is [$84.8M, -$106.9M, $10.6M], a mean of NEGATIVE $3.8M, so about 121% of the recorded base is the after-tax interest add-back on $564.3M of debt. That is the SABR condition in its purest recorded form, and `nonpositive_normalized_fcff` stays silent only because the post-add-back figure is positive by $18M. At the other end, the current run rate is roughly $610M of annualised free cash flow. Between those lie the only two defensible anchors and they disagree: on the 2026 run rate the enterprise is on 2.4x EBITDA and the market requires deeply negative growth, i.e. very cheap; on a through-cycle base drawn from this company's own history — free cash flow of $10.6M, -$106.9M and $84.8M across 2023-25, essentially zero across a full cycle — the enterprise is on roughly 20x and the market requires a great deal, i.e. expensive. Century has destroyed capital across prior cycles, and 2026 is the best year in its history by a factor of twenty. Per the AMR and CSTM rule, when the base is far too low AND the current level is a peak, the answer is the range, not the average.
key_risks: 2026 is the best year in this company's history by roughly 20x: nine-month net income $889.4M against $40.0M a year earlier, and Q4 adjusted EBITDA is already guided DOWN to $275-300M from $331.6M

The margin is policy-dependent — Section 232 tariffs support the Midwest premium and 45X credits sit inside operating cash flow, while the company's own release flags a proposed tariff REDUCTION for parties committing to new US capacity
A greenfield US smelter with $500M of DOE funding and a possible EGA joint venture is undecided and unsized; capex has already more than doubled to $172.2M for nine months
Deloitte issued an ADVERSE opinion on internal control over financial reporting and the Jamalco material weakness was UNREMEDIATED at 2025-12-31, so every number carries reduced confidence
Hurricane Melissa struck Jamalco in late October 2026 and the restart is still in progress — a Q4 disruption not in any reported figure
Through a full cycle this business has generated approximately zero free cash flow: $10.6M, -$106.9M and $84.8M across 2023-25
watch_for: Q4 2026 and Q1 2027 adjusted EBITDA against the $275-300M guide — the test of whether 2026 is a plateau or a spike
The Oklahoma smelter decision and, specifically, Century's own equity contribution net of DOE funding and any EGA partner capital
Any change to Section 232 aluminium tariffs or to the proposed exemption programme for new US capacity commitments
Remediation of the Jamalco material weakness and removal of the adverse ICFR opinion
Jamalco's return to full production after Hurricane Melissa
